narrative:
The model predicted a 75% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess risk, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by your academic performance during law school. Your third-year class ranking was the strongest factor pushing the model toward predicting failure. Standing in the third decile is noticeably lower than the average of accepted students, and this weaker performance in the later stages of your legal studies carried the most weight in the outcome. Your first-year ranking was the second most important factor and also pulled the prediction toward failure, as a fifth-decile placement sits below the average of those who were admitted.

Your LSAT score was the only major factor working in your favor. At 41, it is higher than the average among accepted students, which helped reduce the predicted risk of failure. However, this positive influence was not enough to overcome the stronger negative signals from your law school grades.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.30, middle-income background, and plan to attend full-time were considered but had far less impact on the final prediction.

To improve your chances in future applications, focus on strengthening your academic record if you retake any coursework or pursue additional studies that demonstrate consistent high performance. Consider reapplying once you can show clearer evidence of strong legal reasoning and study skills.
